title.en: Introduction and Syntax of Python Programming

body.en:
Python is a high-level, interpreted, general-purpose programming language known for its simple, readable syntax. It supports procedural, object-oriented and functional programming. It is free and open source and is maintained by the Python Software Foundation (PSF).

What is a scripting language?

A scripting language is a language whose programs (scripts) are executed by an interpreter without a separate compile-and-link step. Scripts are used to automate tasks, glue software components together and build programs quickly. Python, JavaScript, Perl, PHP and shell script are examples. Python is used both as a scripting language and for full-scale applications.

History

  • Python was created by Guido van Rossum at CWI (Centrum Wiskunde & Informatica) in the Netherlands. He started it in December 1989 as a hobby project.
  • The name comes from the BBC comedy show "Monty Python's Flying Circus", not from the snake.
  • It was influenced by the ABC language (and by Modula-3, C and Unix shell).
  • 1991: Python 0.9.0 released, with functions, exception handling, modules and core data types.
  • 1994: Python 1.0, with lambda, map, filter and reduce.
  • 2000: Python 2.0, with list comprehensions, garbage collection and Unicode support.
  • 2008: Python 3.0, a cleaned-up version that is not backward compatible with 2.x (e.g. print became a function).
  • 2020: Python 2 reached end of life (1 January 2020). Today, all new development uses Python 3.
  • Guido van Rossum led the language as its "Benevolent Dictator For Life" until 2018. It is now guided by an elected Steering Council.

1. Simple and easy to learn: English-like syntax with few keywords; programs are short and readable.
  2. Interpreted: code is executed line by line by the interpreter. There is no separate compilation step, and errors are reported as soon as they are reached.
  3. Free and open source: Python can be downloaded, used and distributed freely, and its source code is available.
  4. High-level language: the programmer does not manage memory or hardware details; memory is handled automatically (garbage collection).
  5. Dynamically typed: variables do not need type declarations; the type is decided at run time from the value.
  6. Platform independent (portable): the same program runs on Windows, Linux and macOS without changes.
  7. Object-oriented: supports classes, objects, inheritance and polymorphism. Procedural programming is also supported.
  8. Large standard library ("batteries included"): ready modules for maths, files, dates, networking, databases and more. Thousands of further packages (NumPy, Matplotlib, Django) are available through pip.
  9. Extensible and embeddable: code written in C/C++ can be used in Python, and Python can be embedded in other applications.
  10. Interactive mode: statements can be tested immediately at the >>> prompt.
  11. GUI and database support: Tkinter for GUIs; connectors for MySQL, SQLite and others.

Limitations

  • Slower than compiled languages like C/C++ because it is interpreted.
  • Uses more memory, and is less common for mobile app development.
  • Type errors appear only at run time because of dynamic typing.

AreaExamples / libraries
Web development (server side)Django, Flask; Instagram and Pinterest use Django
Data science and analysisNumPy, Pandas, Matplotlib
Artificial intelligence and machine learningTensorFlow, PyTorch, scikit-learn
Automation and scriptingrenaming files, sending e-mails, web scraping
Desktop GUI applicationsTkinter, PyQt
Game developmentPygame
Scientific and numeric computingSciPy, SymPy
Networking and cyber securitysocket programming, penetration-testing tools
Embedded systems and IoTRaspberry Pi, MicroPython
Software development toolsbuild and testing tools (SCons, pytest)
Educationfirst programming language in many schools and colleges
Blockchain and big datasmart-contract tools, PySpark

Companies using Python include Google, YouTube, NASA, Netflix, Spotify and Dropbox.

Installation steps (Windows)

  1. Open www.python.org → Downloads → download the latest Python 3 installer.
  2. Run the installer and tick "Add python.exe to PATH" (important).
  3. Click Install Now. This installs the interpreter, IDLE (Python's built-in editor) and pip (the package installer).
  4. Verify in the Command Prompt:
C:\> python --version
Python 3.13.0
C:\> pip --version

On Linux, Python 3 is usually pre-installed (python3), or it can be installed with sudo apt install python3.

Ways to run Python code

1. Interactive mode (REPL: Read–Evaluate–Print Loop): type python in the command prompt or open IDLE. Each statement is executed immediately after Enter. It is useful for testing small pieces of code, but the code is not saved.

>>> 5 + 3
8
>>> print("Hello")
Hello
>>> x = 10
>>> x * 2
20
>>> exit()

2. Script mode: write the program in a file with the .py extension and run the whole file. The code is saved and can be reused.

# hello.py  (save the file, then run)
print("Hello, GTU!")

# Command prompt:
# python hello.py      (Windows)
# python3 hello.py     (Linux / macOS)
Interactive modeScript mode
Statement executed immediatelyWhole file executed
Code is not savedCode saved in a .py file
Good for testing and as a calculatorGood for complete programs
Prompt: >>>No prompt

IDEs and editors: IDLE, VS Code, PyCharm, Spyder, Jupyter Notebook. Online: programiz.com, onlinegdb.com.

How a Python program is executed (see diagram)

  1. The source code (.py) is first compiled by the Python compiler into byte code (.pyc files, stored in the __pycache__ folder).
  2. The byte code is executed by the Python Virtual Machine (PVM), the interpreter.
  3. This happens automatically. Because the byte code is platform independent, Python programs are portable.

The standard implementation, written in C, is called CPython. Other implementations include Jython (Java) and PyPy.

h.en: 1.1.5 Basic Structure of a Python Program

body.en:
A Python program may contain the following sections (see diagram). Only the executable statements are compulsory.

  1. Documentation section: comments giving the program name, author and purpose.
  2. Import section: import statements to use modules (math, random, …).
  3. Global declarations: global variables and constants.
  4. Function / class definitions: user-defined functions with def and classes.
  5. Main program: statements that are executed: input, processing, output.
# Program : Area of a circle      <- documentation
# Author  : Ravi Patel

# import section
import math

# global constant
PI = 3.14159

# function definition
def area(r):
    # docstring
    """Return area of circle."""
    return PI * r * r

# main program
r = float(input("Enter radius: "))
print("Area =", area(r))

Comments

# This is a single-line comment
x = 5    # inline comment

"""
This is a multi-line string,
often used as a multi-line comment.
"""

# starts a single-line comment. Python has no special multi-line comment, but a triple-quoted string that is not assigned to anything is often used as one. A triple-quoted string written just after a function header is a docstring (documentation string).

Indentation

Python uses indentation (spaces at the start of a line), not braces { }, to mark a block of code. All statements in a block must have the same indentation; 4 spaces is the standard. A colon : starts a new block.

if marks >= 35:
    # 4 spaces = one block
    print("Pass")
    print("Congratulations")
else:
    print("Fail")
# outside the if block
print("Done")
if x > 0:
# IndentationError: expected an indented block
print("Positive")

Statements and lines

# ; separates statements
a = 5; b = 10; print(a + b)

total = 10 + 20 + \
        # \ continues a line
        30 + 40
nums = [1, 2,
        # inside ( ) [ ] { } no \ needed
        3, 4]
  • No semicolon is needed at the end of a statement; a newline ends it.
  • Python is case-sensitive: Print and print are different.

• Python: high-level, interpreted, dynamically typed, object-oriented, free and open source.
  • Created by Guido van Rossum (CWI, Netherlands), started in 1989 and released in 1991; named after Monty Python.
  • Python 3.0 (2008) is not backward compatible; Python 2 ended in 2020.
  • Applications: web (Django), data science (NumPy, Pandas), AI/ML, automation, GUI, games, IoT.
  • Interactive mode (>>>, not saved) vs script mode (.py file).
  • Execution: source → byte code (.pyc) → PVM.
  • Indentation marks blocks; # starts a comment; no semicolons needed; case-sensitive.

title.en: 1.2 Keywords, Variables, Literals, I/O and Type Casting

body.en:
Keywords

Keywords are reserved words with a predefined meaning. They cannot be used as variable, function or class names. Python 3.13 has 35 keywords; all are lowercase except True, False and None.

CategoryKeywords
ValuesTrue, False, None
Operatorsand, or, not, in, is
Control flowif, elif, else, for, while, break, continue, pass
Functions and classesdef, return, lambda, class, yield, global, nonlocal
Modulesimport, from, as
Exception handlingtry, except, finally, raise, assert
Othersdel, with, async, await
>>> import keyword
# list of all keywords
>>> keyword.kwlist
>>> keyword.iskeyword("if")
True

Identifiers

An identifier is the name given to a variable, function, class or module.

Rules for identifiers:

  1. May contain letters (a–z, A–Z), digits (0–9) and underscore (_).
  2. Must not start with a digit.
  3. No spaces or special symbols (@, $, %, -, etc.).
  4. Must not be a keyword.
  5. They are case-sensitive: Total, total and TOTAL are different.
  6. Any length is allowed.
# Valid identifiers
roll_no   _count   Sum1   totalMarks   MAX_SIZE

# Invalid identifiers
2nd_sem      # starts with a digit
total marks  # contains a space
my-name      # contains a hyphen
for          # keyword

Conventions: variables and functions in lowercase_with_underscores (total_marks); constants in UPPERCASE (PI); classes in CapitalWords (Student). A name starting with an underscore indicates internal use.

A variable is a name that refers to a value (object) stored in memory. In Python a variable is created when a value is first assigned to it; there is no declaration statement.

age = 18             # int
height = 5.6         # float
name = "Kavya"       # str
# same name, now a str (dynamic typing)
age = "eighteen"
print(type(age))     # <class 'str'>

Characteristics

  • Dynamic typing: the type is taken from the value, and the same variable can later refer to a value of another type.
  • A variable is actually a reference to an object. b = a makes both names refer to the same object (see diagram).
  • Every object has an identity (id()), a type (type()) and a value.
  • Using a variable before assigning it gives a NameError.
>>> a = 10
>>> b = a
>>> id(a) == id(b)     # same object
True
>>> a is b
True

Multiple assignment

# same value to many variables
a = b = c = 0
# different values
x, y, z = 10, 20.5, "GTU"
a, b = b, a                # swap

Deleting a variable

x = 100
del x            # deletes the variable
# NameError: name 'x' is not defined
print(x)

A literal is a raw value written directly in a program, e.g. 25, 3.14, "GTU".

Type of literalExamples
IntegerDecimal 25, binary 0b11001, octal 0o31, hexadecimal 0x19
Float3.14, -0.5, 2.5e3 (= 2500.0), 1.5E-2
Complex4+3j, 2j (real + imaginary part with j)
String'single', "double", '''triple''', """multi-line""", raw r"C:\new"
BooleanTrue (1), False (0)
SpecialNone (absence of value)
Collectionlist [1, 2], tuple (1, 2), set {1, 2}, dict {"a": 1}
# Numeric literals
# int (dec, bin, oct, hex)
25    0b11001    0o31    0x19
3.14  2.5e3                        # float
4 + 3j                             # complex

# String literals
'GTU'   "GTU"   """multi-line"""   r"C:\new"

# Boolean and special literals
True   False   None

# Collection literals
[1, 2]   (1, 2)   {1, 2}   {"a": 1}
  • Escape sequences in strings: \n newline, \t tab, \\ backslash, \' and \" quotes.
  • Underscores can be used in numeric literals for readability: 1_00_000.

A constant is a value that should not change while the program runs. Python has no const keyword. By convention, constants are written in UPPERCASE letters, and programmers agree not to modify them.

PI = 3.14159
MAX_STUDENTS = 60
GRAVITY = 9.8
# Python does not stop you changing them,
# so UPPERCASE warns: "do not modify".

Constants are often placed in a separate module and imported:

# constants.py
PI = 3.14159
G = 9.8

# main.py
import constants
print(constants.PI)

Built-in constants include True, False and None. The math module provides math.pi (3.14159…) and math.e (2.71828…).

LiteralConstant
A raw value written in the codeA named value that should not change
3.14159PI = 3.14159

h.en: 1.2.5 Input and Output Functions: input() and print()

body.en:
input()

variable = input("prompt") displays the prompt, waits for the user to type a line and press Enter, and returns the text as a string (str). To use the input as a number, convert it with int() or float().

name = input("Enter name: ")          # str
age = int(input("Enter age: "))       # int
# float
per = float(input("Enter %: "))
# two strings
a, b = input("Two words: ").split()
x, y = map(int, input("Two numbers: ").split())
  • split() breaks the input line at spaces into a list of strings.
  • map(int, …) applies int() to every item.

print()

print(value1, value2, ..., sep=' ', end='\n', file=sys.stdout)
  • Prints one or more values separated by sep (default a space) and finishes with end (default newline '\n').
  • file sends the output to a file instead of the screen.
print("A", "B", 5)              # A B 5
print("A", "B", sep="-")        # A-B
print("Hi", end=" ")            # no newline
# 2025/10/26
print("2025", "10", "26", sep="/")

Formatting output

name, per = "Riya", 77.333
# comma
print("Name:", name, "Per:", per)
# % style
print("Name: %s Per: %.2f" % (name, per))
print("Name: {} Per: {:.2f}".format(name, per))
# f-string
print(f"Name: {name} Per: {per:.2f}")
# width
print(f"{name:>10}|{per:<8.1f}|")
SpecifierMeaning
%d / %f / %sinteger / float / string (old % style)
{:.2f}2 decimal places
{:10} {:<10} {:>10} {:^10}width 10: default / left / right / centre
{:,}thousands separator: 1,00,000 → 100,000

Type conversion means changing a value from one data type to another. There are two types (see diagram).

1. Implicit type conversion

Done automatically by Python when different numeric types are mixed in an expression. The smaller type is converted to the larger type so that no data is lost: bool → int → float → complex.

a = 10        # int
b = 3.5       # float
c = a + b     # int converted to float
print(c, type(c))     # 13.5 <class 'float'>
# 3   (True treated as 1)
print(True + 2)

2. Explicit type conversion (type casting)

Done by the programmer using built-in functions: target_type(value).

FunctionConverts toExample
int(x)integer (truncates decimals)int("25") → 25, int(9.8) → 9
float(x)floating pointfloat("3.5") → 3.5
str(x)stringstr(100) → '100'
bool(x)True / Falsebool(0) → False
complex(a, b)complex numbercomplex(2, 3) → (2+3j)
list(x), tuple(x), set(x)collectionslist("ab") → ['a', 'b']
dict(x)dictionarydict([("a", 1)]) → {'a': 1}
int(s, base)int from a base-2/8/16 stringint("101", 2) → 5
int("25")       # 25
int(9.8)        # 9 (truncates)
float("3.5")    # 3.5
float(7)        # 7.0
str(100)        # '100'
bool(0)         # False
complex(2, 3)   # (2+3j)
int("101", 2)   # 5 (binary to decimal)

Errors in conversion

int("12.5")    # ValueError
int("abc")     # ValueError
# TypeError: can only concatenate str
"Age: " + 18
"Age: " + str(18)   # correct
ImplicitExplicit
Done automatically by PythonDone by the programmer
No data lossData may be lost (int(9.8) → 9)
Only between compatible numeric typesBetween any convertible types

• 35 keywords (Python 3.13); True, False and None are capitalised. Keywords cannot be identifiers.
  • Identifier: letters, digits and _; not starting with a digit; no spaces or symbols; case-sensitive.
  • Variables are created by assignment; they are references to objects; dynamically typed.
  • Literals: integer (dec/bin/oct/hex), float, complex, string, boolean, None, collections.
  • Constants use UPPERCASE by convention (no const keyword).
  • input() always returns str; convert it with int()/float(). print(sep=, end=).
  • Implicit conversion is automatic (int → float); explicit conversion uses int(), float(), str(), bool(), etc.

A data type tells what kind of value a variable holds and which operations can be done on it. In Python, everything is an object, and every value has a type (a class). The type is found with type().

CategoryTypesExample
Numericint, float, complex10, 3.14, 2+3j
BooleanboolTrue, False
Sequencestr, list, tuple (and range)"GTU", [1, 2], (1, 2)
Setset, frozenset{1, 2, 3}
Mappingdict{"a": 1}
None typeNoneTypeNone

Mutable and immutable types

  • Mutable (can be changed after creation): list, set, dict.
  • Immutable (cannot be changed): int, float, complex, bool, str, tuple, frozenset.
lst = [1, 2, 3]
# allowed: list is mutable
lst[0] = 10
tup = (1, 2, 3)
# TypeError: tuple is immutable
tup[0] = 10

Declaration and use: Python has no separate declaration. A variable gets its type when a value is assigned, e.g. x = 5 (int) or x = [5] (list).

• int: whole numbers, positive or negative, with no size limit (limited only by memory). They can be written in decimal, binary (0b), octal (0o) or hexadecimal (0x).
  • float: real numbers with a decimal point or in exponent form, e.g. 3.14 or 1.5e3. Accurate to about 15–17 significant digits, which is why 145/3 prints as 48.333333333333336.
  • complex: numbers of the form a + bj, where j = √−1. Use .real and .imag to get the parts.
  • bool: True or False. bool is a subtype of int: True = 1 and False = 0.
a = 100              # int (no size limit)
# 1267650600228229401496703205376
big = 2 ** 100
b = 3.75             # float
c = 3 + 4j           # complex
# 3.0 4.0 5.0
print(c.real, c.imag, abs(c))
d = True             # bool (subtype of int)
print(True + True)   # 2

A string is an ordered, immutable sequence of characters enclosed in single, double or triple quotes. Python has no separate char type; a single character is a string of length 1.

Declaration

s1 = 'Python'
s2 = "GTU's Diploma"          # ' inside " "
s3 = """Multi
line string"""
s4 = str(123)                 # '123'
empty = ""

Accessing and basic operations

Each character has an index: positive from 0 (left to right) and negative from −1 (right to left). Slicing s[start:end:step] extracts part of a string; the end index is excluded (see diagram).

s = "PYTHON"
s[0]        # 'P'      first
s[-1]       # 'N'      last
s[1:4]      # 'YTH'    slicing
"Py" + "thon"   # 'Python'  concatenation
"Hi " * 3       # 'Hi Hi Hi '  repetition
"TH" in s       # True     membership
len(s)          # 6

Immutability

s = "Python"
s[0] = "J"         # TypeError: immutable
s = "J" + s[1:]    # 'Jython' – a new string

String methods such as upper(), lower(), replace(), find() and split() are covered in Unit 4.

A list is an ordered, mutable collection of items written in square brackets [ ] and separated by commas.

  • It can contain items of different types, and duplicates are allowed.
  • Items are accessed by index (0, 1, … or −1, −2, …) and slicing.
  • Items can be added, changed and removed after creation.
marks = [78, 85, 62]          # create
mixed = [1, "two", 3.5, True]
empty = []
marks[0]          # 78     access
marks[1] = 90     # update -> [78, 90, 62]
# add    -> [78, 90, 62, 70]
marks.append(70)
del marks[2]      # delete -> [78, 90, 70]
len(marks)        # 3

Uses: a collection of marks, names or any items that may change. Lists are covered in detail in Unit 3.

A tuple is an ordered, immutable collection of items written in parentheses ( ).

  • Like a list it is indexed and allows duplicates and mixed types, but its items cannot be changed, added or removed.
  • A single-item tuple needs a trailing comma: (5,). Without the comma, (5) is just the int 5.
  • It is faster and uses less memory than a list, and it can be used as a dictionary key.
t = (10, 20, 30)          # create
# parentheses optional
t2 = 1, 2, 3
# single item: comma needed
one = (5,)
t[0]          # 10       access
t[1:]         # (20, 30)
t[0] = 99     # TypeError: immutable
del t         # whole tuple can be deleted

Uses: fixed data such as days of the week, (x, y) coordinates or RGB colours.

A set is an unordered collection of unique items written in curly braces { }.

  • No duplicates: repeated values are stored only once.
  • No indexing or slicing, because there is no fixed order.
  • The set itself is mutable (items can be added or removed), but its items must be immutable (numbers, strings, tuples).
  • An empty set is created with set(); {} creates an empty dictionary.
  • It supports mathematical set operations: union |, intersection &, difference -, symmetric difference ^.
  • frozenset is an immutable version of a set.
# {1, 2, 3} duplicates removed
s = {3, 1, 2, 3}
# empty set ({} is a dict!)
e = set()
s.add(5)                 # add
# delete (error if missing)
s.remove(1)
s.discard(9)             # delete (no error)
2 in s                   # True
# TypeError: not subscriptable
s[0]

Uses: removing duplicates, membership testing, finding common items.

A dictionary is a mutable collection of key: value pairs written in curly braces { }. Values are accessed by key, not by index.

  • Keys must be unique and immutable (str, int, tuple); values can be of any type and may repeat.
  • It keeps insertion order (from Python 3.7).
  • Assigning to a new key adds a pair; assigning to an existing key updates its value.
d = {"roll": 101, "name": "Amit"}   # create
# 'Amit'   access by key
d["name"]
d.get("city", "-")   # '-'      safe access
d["sem"] = 2         # add new pair
d["name"] = "Riya"   # update
del d["roll"]        # delete a pair
d.keys()   d.values()   d.items()

Uses: records (student details), word counts, phone books, configuration settings.

body.en:
PropertyListTupleSetDictionary
Brackets[ ]( ){ }{key: value}
OrderedYesYesNoYes (3.7+)
MutableYesNoYesYes
DuplicatesAllowedAllowedNot allowedKeys unique
IndexingBy positionBy positionNot possibleBy key
Empty[] or list()() or tuple()set(){} or dict()
Example[1, 2, 2](1, 2, 2){1, 2}{"a": 1}
UseChanging collectionFixed dataUnique itemsKey-based lookup

• Everything in Python is an object; type() gives its class.
  • Numeric: int (unlimited size), float, complex (a+bj); bool is a subtype of int (True = 1).
  • str: immutable, ordered sequence of characters; indexing from 0 and −1; slicing [start:end:step] with end excluded.
  • list [ ]: ordered, mutable, allows duplicates.
  • tuple ( ): ordered, immutable; single item needs a comma: (5,).
  • set { }: unordered, unique items, no indexing; empty set = set().
  • dict {k: v}: key-value pairs; keys unique and immutable; empty dict = {}.
  • Mutable: list, set, dict. Immutable: int, float, complex, bool, str, tuple, frozenset.

title.en: First Python program and print() options

code.en:
# My first Python program
print("Hello, World!")
# values separated by space
print("Welcome to", "GTU", "Diploma")
# custom separator
print("A", "B", "C", sep="-")
# no newline at end
print("Python", end=" ")
print("is easy")
# escape sequences
print("Line1\nLine2\tTabbed")
# blank line
print()
print('Single quotes', "double quotes", """triple quotes""")

programs.out:
Hello, World!
Welcome to GTU Diploma
A-B-C
Python is easy
Line1
Line2	Tabbed

Single quotes double quotes triple quotes

expl.en:
• A Python program needs no main(), header files or semicolons. Statements run from top to bottom.
  • print() separates values with a space by default. sep changes the separator and end changes what is printed at the end (default '\n').
  • \n = newline, \t = tab. Strings may use single, double or triple quotes.
  • Text after # is a comment and is ignored by the interpreter.

code.en:
name = input("Enter your name      : ")
contact = input("Enter contact number : ")
email = input("Enter email          : ")
dob = input("Enter birth date     : ")

print("\n------ Student Details ------")
print("Name      :", name)
print("Contact   :", contact)
print("Email     :", email)
print("Birth date:", dob)
print("-----------------------------")

programs.out:
Enter your name      : Ravi Patel
Enter contact number : 9876543210
Enter email          : ravi.patel@gmail.com
Enter birth date     : 15-08-2008

------ Student Details ------
Name      : Ravi Patel
Contact   : 9876543210
Email     : ravi.patel@gmail.com
Birth date: 15-08-2008
-----------------------------

expl.en: input(prompt) shows the prompt, waits for the user to type and press Enter, and returns the text as a string. Here all four values are kept as strings because no calculation is needed. A contact number is stored as a string so that leading zeros and the + sign are not lost.

title.en: Sum and average of three numbers

code.en:
a = int(input("Enter first number : "))
b = int(input("Enter second number: "))
c = int(input("Enter third number : "))

total = a + b + c
avg = total / 3

print("Sum     =", total)
print("Average =", avg)
print("Average (2 decimals) = %.2f" % avg)
print(f"Average using f-string = {avg:.2f}")

programs.out:
Enter first number : 45
Enter second number: 62
Enter third number : 38
Sum     = 145
Average = 48.333333333333336
Average (2 decimals) = 48.33
Average using f-string = 48.33

expl.en:
• input() returns a string, so int() converts it to an integer before adding. Without it, "45" + "62" would join the strings to give "4562".
  • / always gives a float in Python 3 (145 / 3 = 48.333…).
  • Formatting to 2 decimal places: the old style "%.2f" % value, or an f-string f"{value:.2f}".

title.en: Area and circumference of a circle

code.en:
# constant (by convention)
PI = 3.14159

r = float(input("Enter radius: "))
area = PI * r * r
circum = 2 * PI * r

print("Area          =", round(area, 2))
print("Circumference =", round(circum, 2))

expl.en: float() allows decimal input such as 7.5. Python has no const keyword, so constants are written in UPPERCASE by convention (PI), and the programmer must not change them. round(x, 2) rounds to 2 decimal places.

code.en:
p = float(input("Principal amount (Rs): "))
r = float(input("Rate of interest (%) : "))
n = float(input("Time (years)         : "))

si = (p * r * n) / 100
amount = p + si

print("Simple Interest = Rs", si)
print("Total Amount    = Rs", amount)

programs.out:
Principal amount (Rs): 25000
Rate of interest (%) : 8.5
Time (years)         : 3
Simple Interest = Rs 6375.0
Total Amount    = Rs 31375.0

expl.en: Formula: SI = P × R × N / 100. Each input is converted with float() because rates and amounts may contain decimals. Arithmetic follows normal mathematical precedence; the parentheses make the order clear.

code.en:
a = int(input("Enter a: "))
b = int(input("Enter b: "))
print("Before swap: a =", a, " b =", b)

# Method 1: using a third variable
temp = a
a = b
b = temp
print("After method 1: a =", a, " b =", b)

# Method 2: without a third variable
a = a + b
b = a - b
a = a - b
print("After method 2: a =", a, " b =", b)

# Method 3: Pythonic way (tuple unpacking)
a, b = b, a
print("After method 3: a =", a, " b =", b)

programs.out:
Enter a: 10
Enter b: 25
Before swap: a = 10  b = 25
After method 1: a = 25  b = 10
After method 2: a = 10  b = 25
After method 3: a = 25  b = 10

expl.en: Method 3 is unique to Python: a, b = b, a first builds the tuple (b, a) on the right side, then assigns its items to a and b. This is called multiple assignment or tuple unpacking. Each method swaps the values once, so the output alternates.

title.en: Data types with type() and isinstance()

code.en:
a = 25
b = 3.75
c = 2 + 5j
d = "Python"
e = True
f = [10, 20, 30]
g = (1, 2, 3)
h = {1, 2, 3}
i = {"roll": 101, "name": "Amit"}
j = None

for value in (a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, i, j):
    print(repr(value).ljust(30), type(value))

print("isinstance(a, int)   :", isinstance(a, int))
print("isinstance(b, float) :", isinstance(b, float))
print("Real/imag part of c  :", c.real, c.imag)

programs.out:
25                             <class 'int'>
3.75                           <class 'float'>
(2+5j)                         <class 'complex'>
'Python'                       <class 'str'>
True                           <class 'bool'>
[10, 20, 30]                   <class 'list'>
(1, 2, 3)                      <class 'tuple'>
{1, 2, 3}                      <class 'set'>
{'roll': 101, 'name': 'Amit'}  <class 'dict'>
None                           <class 'NoneType'>
isinstance(a, int)   : True
isinstance(b, float) : True
Real/imag part of c  : 2.0 5.0

expl.en:
• Python is dynamically typed: the type is decided from the value at run time, so no declaration is needed.
  • type(x) returns the class of the value. isinstance(x, T) checks whether x is of type T.
  • repr() shows the value as Python code (strings in quotes) and ljust(30) pads it to 30 characters so that the output lines up.
  • A complex number has .real and .imag parts; Python uses j for the imaginary unit.

title.en: Type casting: implicit and explicit conversion

code.en:
# Implicit conversion (done automatically)
x = 10          # int
y = 2.5         # float
z = x + y       # int is promoted to float
print("10 + 2.5 =", z, type(z))
print("True + 5 =", True + 5)

# Explicit conversion (done by programmer)
print('int("25")     =', int("25"))
# decimal part removed
print("int(9.99)     =", int(9.99))
print('float("3.5")  =', float("3.5"))
print("float(7)      =", float(7))
print("str(100)      =", repr(str(100)))
print("bool(0), bool(5)    =", bool(0), bool(5))
print('bool(""), bool("a") =', bool(""), bool("a"))
print("complex(2, 3) =", complex(2, 3))
print('list("GTU")   =', list("GTU"))
print("tuple([1, 2]) =", tuple([1, 2]))
print("set([1,1,2])  =", set([1, 1, 2]))
# binary string to int
print('int("1010", 2)=', int("1010", 2))

try:
    int("12.5")
except ValueError as err:
    print("Error:", err)

programs.out:
10 + 2.5 = 12.5 <class 'float'>
True + 5 = 6
int("25")     = 25
int(9.99)     = 9
float("3.5")  = 3.5
float(7)      = 7.0
str(100)      = '100'
bool(0), bool(5)    = False True
bool(""), bool("a") = False True
complex(2, 3) = (2+3j)
list("GTU")   = ['G', 'T', 'U']
tuple([1, 2]) = (1, 2)
set([1,1,2])  = {1, 2}
int("1010", 2)= 10
Error: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '12.5'

expl.en:
• Implicit conversion: in mixed expressions Python converts the lower type to the higher type (bool → int → float → complex) so that no data is lost.
  • Explicit conversion (type casting): done using functions like int(), float(), str(), bool(), list(), tuple(), set() and complex().
  • int(9.99) truncates to 9 (it does not round). bool() is False for 0, empty strings and empty collections, and True otherwise.
  • A string that is not a valid integer, such as "12.5", raises a ValueError. Here it is caught with try/except so the program can continue.

code.en:
c = float(input("Enter temperature in Celsius: "))
f = c * 9 / 5 + 32
print(f"{c} °C = {f:.1f} °F")

f = float(input("Enter temperature in Fahrenheit: "))
c = (f - 32) * 5 / 9
print(f"{f} °F = {c:.1f} °C")

programs.out:
Enter temperature in Celsius: 37
37.0 °C = 98.6 °F
Enter temperature in Fahrenheit: 98.6
98.6 °F = 37.0 °C

expl.en: Formulas: F = C × 9/5 + 32 and C = (F − 32) × 5/9. Inside an f-string, {f:.1f} prints the value with 1 decimal place. The same variable can be reused for a new value, because a variable is just a name for an object.

title.en: String operations: index, slice, join, repeat

code.en:
s = "PYTHON"
print("String      :", s)
print("Length      :", len(s))
print("s[0], s[-1] :", s[0], s[-1])
print("s[2:5]      :", s[2:5])
print("s[:3]       :", s[:3])
print("s[3:]       :", s[3:])
print("s[::-1]     :", s[::-1])

first = "Diploma"
second = "Engineering"
print("Concatenate :", first + " " + second)
print("Repeat      :", "Hi! " * 3)
print("Membership  :", "PY" in s, "Java" in s)
print("Upper/lower :", first.upper(), first.lower())

name = input("Enter your name: ")
print("Hello " + name + ", your name has", len(name), "characters.")

programs.out:
String      : PYTHON
Length      : 6
s[0], s[-1] : P N
s[2:5]      : THO
s[:3]       : PYT
s[3:]       : HON
s[::-1]     : NOHTYP
Concatenate : Diploma Engineering
Repeat      : Hi! Hi! Hi! 
Membership  : True False
Upper/lower : DIPLOMA diploma
Enter your name: Kavya
Hello Kavya, your name has 5 characters.

expl.en:
• Characters are accessed by index: positive from 0 (left) and negative from −1 (right). See the diagram "String Indexing and Slicing".
  • Slicing s[start:end:step] gives the characters from start up to end − 1. s[::-1] reverses the string.
  • + joins (concatenates) strings, * repeats them, and in checks whether a substring is present.
  • Strings are immutable: methods like upper() return a new string and leave the original unchanged.

code.en:
marks = [78, 85, 62, 90]
print("List          :", marks)
print("First, last   :", marks[0], marks[-1])
print("Slice [1:3]   :", marks[1:3])

# update an element
marks[2] = 70
print("After update  :", marks)

# add at end
marks.append(88)
# add at index 1
marks.insert(1, 55)
print("After add     :", marks)

# delete by value
marks.remove(55)
# delete by index
del marks[0]
print("After delete  :", marks)

print("Length, sum   :", len(marks), sum(marks))
print("Max, min      :", max(marks), min(marks))
# different types allowed
mixed = [1, "two", 3.0, True]
print("Mixed list    :", mixed)

programs.out:
List          : [78, 85, 62, 90]
First, last   : 78 90
Slice [1:3]   : [85, 62]
After update  : [78, 85, 70, 90]
After add     : [78, 55, 85, 70, 90, 88]
After delete  : [85, 70, 90, 88]
Length, sum   : 4 333
Max, min      : 90 70
Mixed list    : [1, 'two', 3.0, True]

expl.en: A list is an ordered, mutable collection written in square brackets. It can hold values of different types and allows duplicates. Elements can be changed with an index, added with append()/insert(), and removed with remove() (by value) or del (by index). Lists are covered in detail in Unit 3.

title.en: Tuple and set: create, access, update, delete

code.en:
# Tuple: ordered, immutable
t = (10, 20, 30, 20)
print("Tuple         :", t)
print("t[1], t[-1]   :", t[1], t[-1])
print("count(20)     :", t.count(20))
print("index(30)     :", t.index(30))
# comma needed for one item
single = (5,)
print("Single tuple  :", single, type(single))
try:
    # not allowed
    t[0] = 99
except TypeError as e:
    print("Update error  :", e)
# create a new tuple instead
t = t + (40,)
print("New tuple     :", t)

# Set: unordered, unique items, mutable
s = {3, 1, 2, 3, 1}
# duplicates removed
print("Set           :", s)
s.add(5)
s.discard(1)
print("After add/del :", s)
print("2 in s        :", 2 in s)
a, b = {1, 2, 3}, {2, 3, 4}
print("Union a | b   :", a | b)
print("Intersection  :", a & b)

expl.en:
• A tuple ( ) is like a list but immutable: its items cannot be changed, added or removed. A new tuple must be created instead. A single-item tuple needs a trailing comma: (5,).
  • A set { } stores unique items in no fixed order, so duplicates are removed automatically and indexing is not possible. It supports mathematical operations such as union | and intersection &.
  • Small integers are printed in sorted order here, but the order of a set is not guaranteed.

code.en:
student = {"roll": 101, "name": "Amit", "branch": "Computer"}
print("Dictionary   :", student)
print("Name         :", student["name"])
print("get('city')  :", student.get("city", "Not found"))

# add a new key
student["sem"] = 2
# update a value
student["name"] = "Amit Shah"
print("After update :", student)

# delete a key
del student["branch"]
print("After delete :", student)

print("Keys   :", list(student.keys()))
print("Values :", list(student.values()))
for key, value in student.items():
    print(f"  {key:5} -> {value}")

expl.en:
• A dictionary stores key: value pairs in braces. Values are accessed by key, not by position.
  • Keys must be unique and immutable (e.g. str, int, tuple); values can be of any type.
  • Assigning to a new key adds it, and assigning to an existing key updates it. del removes a key. get() returns a default value instead of raising an error if the key is missing.
  • keys(), values() and items() give the keys, the values and the pairs.

programs.out:
Total keywords: 35
['False', 'None', 'True', 'and', 'as', 'assert', 'async', 'await', 'break', 'class', 'continue', 'def', 'del', 'elif', 'else', 'except', 'finally', 'for', 'from', 'global', 'if', 'import', 'in', 'is', 'lambda', 'nonlocal', 'not', 'or', 'pass', 'raise', 'return', 'try', 'while', 'with', 'yield']
roll_no      : valid
_count       : valid
2nd_sem      : invalid
total marks  : invalid
for          : invalid (keyword)
Sum1         : valid
my-name      : invalid

expl.en:
• Keywords are reserved words with a special meaning, so they cannot be used as names. Python 3.13 has 35 keywords. True, False and None start with a capital letter.
  • Identifier rules: use letters, digits and underscore only; do not start with a digit; no spaces or special symbols; not a keyword. Identifiers are case-sensitive (Sum1 and sum1 are different).
  • str.isidentifier() checks the naming rules and keyword.iskeyword() checks for keywords.

title.en: Literals: number systems, strings, boolean, None

code.en:
# Integer literals in different number systems
dec = 25
binary = 0b11001
octal = 0o31
hexa = 0x19
print("Decimal, binary, octal, hex:", dec, binary, octal, hexa)
print("bin(25), oct(25), hex(25)  :", bin(25), oct(25), hex(25))

# Float and complex literals
print("Float literals   :", 3.14, 2.5e3, 1.5E-2)
print("Complex literal  :", 4 + 3j)
# underscores allowed
print("Readable number  :", 1_00_000)

# String literals
single = 'GTU'
multi = """Line one
Line two"""
# raw: \ not special
raw = r"C:\new\test"
print(single, "|", raw)
print(multi)

# Boolean and special literals
print("Boolean :", True, False, True + True)
print("None    :", None, type(None))

programs.out:
Decimal, binary, octal, hex: 25 25 25 25
bin(25), oct(25), hex(25)  : 0b11001 0o31 0x19
Float literals   : 3.14 2500.0 0.015
Complex literal  : (4+3j)
Readable number  : 100000
GTU | C:\new\test
Line one
Line two
Boolean : True False 2
None    : None <class 'NoneType'>

expl.en:
• A literal is a fixed value written directly in the code.
  • Integer literals can be decimal, binary (0b), octal (0o) or hexadecimal (0x). All four above are the same number, 25. bin(), oct() and hex() convert the other way.
  • Float literals can use exponent form: 2.5e3 = 2500.0. Underscores make big numbers readable.
  • String literals: single, double, triple (multi-line) and raw (r"", where backslashes are not escape characters).
  • Boolean literals: True (1) and False (0). Special literal: None, meaning "no value".

title.en: Formatted output: marksheet with f-strings and format()

code.en:
name = input("Student name: ")
m1, m2, m3 = map(int, input("Marks of 3 subjects: ").split())

total = m1 + m2 + m3
per = total / 3

print("\n{:^30}".format("MARKSHEET"))
print("-" * 30)
print(f"{'Name':<12}: {name}")
print(f"{'Subject 1':<12}: {m1:>5}")
print(f"{'Subject 2':<12}: {m2:>5}")
print(f"{'Subject 3':<12}: {m3:>5}")
print("-" * 30)
print(f"{'Total':<12}: {total:>5}")
print(f"{'Percentage':<12}: {per:>8.2f} %")
print("Result: %s with %.1f%%" % (name, per))

programs.out:
Student name: Riya Shah
Marks of 3 subjects: 78 85 69

          MARKSHEET           
------------------------------
Name        : Riya Shah
Subject 1   :    78
Subject 2   :    85
Subject 3   :    69
------------------------------
Total       :   232
Percentage  :    77.33 %
Result: Riya Shah with 77.3%

expl.en:
• input().split() splits the line "78 85 69" into three strings. map(int, …) converts each one to int, and they are assigned to m1, m2, m3 in one line.
  • Alignment in format specifiers: < left, > right, ^ centre; :>8.2f means right-aligned, width 8, 2 decimals.
  • Three ways to format output: f-strings f"{x}" (Python 3.6+), str.format(), and the old % operator (%% prints a % sign).

title.en: How a Python Program is Executed
Basic Structure of a Python Program
List vs Tuple vs Set vs Dictionary

q.en: What is Python?

a.en: A high-level, interpreted, general-purpose, dynamically typed and object-oriented programming language.

q.en: Who developed Python and when?

a.en: Guido van Rossum at CWI, Netherlands. He started in 1989 and the first release (0.9.0) was in 1991.

q.en: Why is it named Python?

a.en: After the BBC comedy show "Monty Python's Flying Circus".

q.en: What is a scripting language?

a.en: A language whose programs (scripts) are executed directly by an interpreter without a separate compilation step, e.g. Python, JavaScript, Perl.

q.en: Is Python compiled or interpreted?

a.en: Both, internally. Source code is compiled to byte code (.pyc), which is executed by the Python Virtual Machine (interpreter). It is generally called an interpreted language.

q.en: What is PVM?

a.en: The Python Virtual Machine, which executes Python byte code.

q.en: What is byte code?

a.en: Low-level, platform-independent code produced by compiling .py files; stored in .pyc files.

q.en: List any five features of Python.

a.en: Simple, interpreted, free and open source, dynamically typed, portable, object-oriented, large standard library.

q.en: Give applications of Python.

a.en: Web development (Django, Flask), data science, AI/ML, automation, GUI apps, games, IoT and scientific computing.

q.en: Difference between Python 2 and Python 3?

a.en: Python 3 is not backward compatible: print is a function, / gives a float result, and strings are Unicode by default. Python 2 ended in 2020.

q.en: What is IDLE?

a.en: Integrated Development and Learning Environment: Python's built-in editor and shell.

q.en: What is pip?

a.en: Python's package installer, used to install external libraries, e.g. pip install numpy.

q.en: Difference between interactive mode and script mode?

a.en: Interactive mode runs each statement immediately at the >>> prompt and does not save the code; script mode runs a saved .py file.

q.en: What is the extension of a Python file?

a.en: .py (byte code files use .pyc).

q.en: How are blocks defined in Python?

a.en: By indentation (usually 4 spaces) after a colon, instead of braces.

q.en: What happens if indentation is wrong?

a.en: Python raises an IndentationError.

q.en: How do you write comments in Python?

a.en: # for single-line comments; triple-quoted strings are often used for multi-line comments and docstrings.

q.en: What is a docstring?

a.en: A triple-quoted string written as the first statement of a module, function or class, used as its documentation.

q.en: What are keywords? How many are there?

a.en: Reserved words with a special meaning. Python 3.13 has 35 keywords.

q.en: Which keywords start with a capital letter?

a.en: True, False and None.

q.en: What is an identifier? Give its rules.

a.en: A name for a variable, function or class. It may use letters, digits and _, must not start with a digit, cannot contain spaces or symbols, cannot be a keyword, and is case-sensitive.

q.en: Is Python case-sensitive?

a.en: Yes. Total and total are different names.

q.en: What is a variable in Python?

a.en: A name that refers to an object in memory. It is created when a value is assigned.

q.en: What is dynamic typing?

a.en: The type of a variable is decided at run time from the value assigned, and it can change.

q.en: How do you swap two variables in Python?

a.en: a, b = b, a

q.en: What does id() return?

a.en: The identity (unique number, related to the memory address) of an object.

q.en: What is a literal?

a.en: A fixed value written directly in code, e.g. 10, 3.14, 'GTU', True, None.

q.en: How are binary, octal and hex literals written?

a.en: With the prefixes 0b, 0o and 0x, e.g. 0b101, 0o17, 0x1F.

q.en: How are constants created in Python?

a.en: There is no const keyword. Names are written in UPPERCASE by convention, e.g. PI = 3.14.

q.en: What is None?

a.en: A special literal meaning "no value". Its type is NoneType.

q.en: What does input() return?

a.en: Always a string (str).

q.en: How do you read an integer?

a.en: n = int(input("Enter n: "))

q.en: What are sep and end in print()?

a.en: sep is the separator between values (default a space); end is printed at the end (default newline).

q.en: What is an f-string?

a.en: A formatted string literal prefixed with f, where expressions in braces are replaced by their values, e.g. f"Sum = {a+b}".

q.en: What is type casting?

a.en: Converting a value from one data type to another using functions like int(), float(), str().

q.en: Difference between implicit and explicit conversion?

a.en: Implicit conversion is done automatically by Python (int to float in 3 + 2.5); explicit conversion is done by the programmer (int("25")).

q.en: What is int(7.9)?

a.en: 7. int() truncates the decimal part; it does not round.

q.en: What happens with int("12.5")?

a.en: ValueError, because "12.5" is not a valid integer string. Use int(float("12.5")).

q.en: Name the built-in data types of Python.

a.en: Numeric (int, float, complex), bool, sequence (str, list, tuple), set (set, frozenset), mapping (dict) and NoneType.

q.en: Which data types are mutable?

a.en: list, set and dict.

q.en: Which data types are immutable?

a.en: int, float, complex, bool, str, tuple and frozenset.

q.en: Is there a char data type in Python?

a.en: No. A single character is a string of length 1.

q.en: What is negative indexing?

a.en: Accessing items from the end: -1 is the last item, -2 the second last.

q.en: What is slicing?

a.en: Extracting a part of a sequence with [start:end:step]; the end index is excluded.

q.en: Difference between list and tuple?

a.en: A list is mutable and uses [ ]; a tuple is immutable, uses ( ) and is faster.

q.en: How do you create a tuple with one item?

a.en: With a trailing comma: t = (5,)

q.en: What is a set?

a.en: An unordered collection of unique items in { }; it supports union and intersection.

q.en: How do you create an empty set?

a.en: set(). {} creates an empty dictionary.

q.en: What is a dictionary?

a.en: A mutable collection of key: value pairs; values are accessed by key.

q.en: Can a list be a dictionary key?

a.en: No. Keys must be immutable; a tuple can be used instead.
